name: OneTab
tagline: Browser extension that collapses a wall of open tabs into a single list you can restore later, with a paid tier for syncing those lists across devices.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The free part of OneTab, take all my tabs, dump them into one list, let me restore them one by one, is close to a textbook one-shot: a MV3 extension, chrome.tabs.query, chrome.storage.local, and a list page. An agent will get that working in a single session and you will probably like your version better because you can add tags and search. The paid thing here is sync, and sync is where DIY gets honest: you need a server, a token, conflict handling when two machines both archive at once, and a plan for when your laptop has been offline for a week. None of that is hard, it is just not one sitting, and it is forever yours to babysit. Build it if you mostly want local archiving; pay if the entire point is that the list is identical on four machines.
coreLoopDIY: Collapses every tab in the current window into a timestamped, named, searchable list stored locally, restores items or whole lists with one click, and optionally pushes the archive to a self-hosted endpoint you own.
requirements: Chrome or any Chromium browser with developer mode for unpacked extensions
Node 20 if you want the optional sync server
A small always-on box or cheap VPS to host the sync endpoint
A shared bearer token in .env on each device
whatYouLose: Sync that already works, including the boring cases: offline devices, two machines archiving at once, a list with 3,000 entries
Install and auto-update through the extension stores, plus Firefox and Safari builds you did not have to port yourself
The shareable public web page for a tab list, which people use more than they admit
Years of restore-reliability hardening; nothing stings like a one-click restore that loses half the list
Import of your existing OneTab archive, unless you write the parser too
moatNotes: The archive is the lock-in. Thousands of saved tabs going back years are an awkward thing to migrate, and the sync tier exists precisely because that pile now lives in two places.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because tab hoarders are not shopping for a tab manager, they are protecting an archive. Once a few thousand links are in there the question stops being which extension is nicer and becomes whether the thing will still be there, on every machine, after a browser update. A paid sync tier on a tool that has been around for over a decade answers that more cheaply than a self-hosted endpoint you maintain alone, and the price is low enough that nobody runs the build-versus-buy math seriously.
notes: The tab collapser is an afternoon; the trust that your 4,000 saved links survive a sync is what the money buys.
prompt:
Build a Chrome MV3 extension called TabVault in this empty folder. Plain JavaScript, no build step, no framework, no bundler.

Core behavior:
- Toolbar button opens a popup with three actions: Archive this window, Archive all windows, Open vault.
- Archiving grabs every normal tab (skip chrome:// and extension pages), saves title and URL, closes those tabs, and leaves one tab open on the vault page.
- Each archive is a list: id, createdAt, optional name, array of items with title, url, and addedAt.
- Storage is chrome.storage.local only. No accounts, no analytics, no remote calls unless sync is explicitly configured.

Vault page (vault.html, served from the extension):
- Lists archives newest first, collapsible, with item count and relative date.
- Per item: open in new tab and remove from list. Per list: restore all, restore all and delete, rename, delete, pin to top.
- Full text search across titles and URLs with instant filtering.
- Export and import the whole vault as JSON.
- Dedupe toggle: when archiving, drop URLs already present in any pinned list.

Optional self-hosted sync, built as a separate folder server/:
- Node 20 plus Express, single file, stores the vault JSON on disk at a path from .env.
- Two routes: GET /vault returns the JSON blob and its version number, PUT /vault accepts a blob and an expected version and rejects on mismatch with 409.
- Auth is one bearer token read from .env. Ship .env.example, never a real token.
- Extension side: a settings panel for server URL and token, a manual Sync now button, last-sync timestamp, and a merge strategy that unions lists by id and keeps the newer name on conflict. Last write wins per list, and say so in the UI.

Explicitly out of scope: Firefox and Safari builds, store packaging, background auto-sync timers, multi-user auth, encryption at rest.

Finish with a README covering loading the unpacked extension, running the sync server, and where the data physically lives.
